excerpt: Section 4, Model Description (paraphrased for practice). Consider a layer with outputs y^(l). With dropout, the feed-forward operation becomes r_j^(l) ~ Bernoulli(p), ỹ^(l) = r^(l) * y^(l), z_i^(l+1) = w_i^(l+1) ỹ^(l) + b_i^(l+1), y_i^(l+1) = f(z_i^(l+1)), where * is an element-wise product and r^(l) is a vector of independent Bernoulli random variables, each equal to 1 with probability p. Each unit is therefore retained with probability p and dropped otherwise, and a different thinned network is sampled for every training case. At test time it is not feasible to average the predictions of exponentially many thinned networks, so a single network without dropout is used whose weights are scaled versions of the trained weights: if a unit is retained with probability p during training, its outgoing weights are multiplied by p at test time (W_test = p W). This ensures that for any hidden unit the expected output under the training-time distribution equals the actual output at test time (Section 4, Figure 2).
focus: Explain why weights are multiplied by the retention probability p at test time. Use one output unit z = Σ w_j r_j y_j with a handful of inputs (at most 6). Let the learner change p, the inputs y and the weights w, and step through several deterministic sample masks r (use a fixed, seeded pseudo-random sequence so results are reproducible). Show the thinned outputs for each mask, their running average, the exact expectation p·Σ w_j y_j, and the test-time output with W_test = pW. Guide them through p = 1 (no dropout) and p = 0.5. Check that the exact expectation equals the test-time output for every p, and that the average over all 2ⁿ masks weighted by their probabilities equals it too.
audience: Second-year engineering undergraduates who know weighted sums and expected value but not neural network training.
